title: Augmented visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback in motor learning: A review
extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical review of augmented feedback in motor learning, asking how human- or technology-provided feedback can best support learning and performance in motor tasks. It synthesizes prior research on visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback, with particular attention to when concurrent feedback helps or hinders learning, and how task complexity changes these effects.

The review covers a wide range of motor-learning contexts, including sports, rehabilitation, and laboratory-based movement tasks. Although it mainly discusses studies with healthy adults, it also notes some rehabilitation studies with patients. The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it compares feedback strategies such as concurrent versus terminal feedback, feedback frequency, self-controlled feedback, bandwidth and fading schedules, and different visualization or sonification designs.

The main conclusion is that feedback effectiveness depends heavily on task complexity, learner skill level, modality, and display design. Concurrent visual feedback often helps early learning in complex tasks but can impair retention in simple tasks if it creates dependency. Auditory and haptic feedback may reduce visual overload and offer useful alternatives, but their mappings must be intuitive. Overall, the paper argues for carefully designed, task-specific, and modality-appropriate feedback systems that support learning without creating overreliance on the external feedback source.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical review, not an empirical study with a defined experimental design, sample, or causal estimation. It is peer-reviewed academic literature, but it does not provide direct evidence for the requested school-based AI lesson-plan feedback or instructional coaching use case.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test an intervention in the education domain and reports no measurable effect on the target outcomes. Its relevance to the retrieved topic is only indirect and conceptual, so there is no demonstrable impact on teacher feedback workflows.

interventions.use_case: The paper is a theoretical review of augmented feedback modalities in motor learning, including visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback systems for sports and rehabilitation training; it does not evaluate an education-specific AI tutoring workflow.
